note: W1-LIBRARY round 2. A fourth multi-volume series, written to close a measured hole rather than to decorate: the corpus had NO books between 944 and 1,316 words, so RI-LOR03 step 1's p90 read 1,316 on book-stats.py's floor-index percentile and 1,167 under linear interpolation, and the round-1 critic caught S1b passing by choice of estimator. The estimator is fixed; these are the books that make the real number pass. They also give T4 (diary/letters/ledgers) three entries it was short of and put an Imperial COURT in the library, which the corpus had described from outside (the-lease-and-what-it-costs, the-blessings-of-the-coast, ledger-leaf) and never from the bench. Merrow adjudicates nothing that the library adjudicates elsewhere: he cannot decide the seventeen and says so, which is RI-LOR06's convention rather than an exception to it.

books.title: The Casebook of the Assize at Gideon, Volume the First: Of the Forms
books.author: Justiciar Aulus Merrow, of the Assize at Gideon, in his own hand and not for the Office
books.unreliability: An honest, careful, self-examining record by a man who believes that a person who does not complain has nothing to complain of, and who is told twice in three volumes that this is not how the province speaks. He writes down every warning and changes nothing.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Treats silence as evidence. He records that a poler asked twice by the court said nothing and reasons that 'a man who has a grievance says so when a court asks him twice' — in a province whose coastal custom, set down in a-progress-ii and confirmed to him by his own interpreter, is that repeating a question is an accusation and that the polite answer is the smaller one. He is also wrong that no offence is disclosed by a stone he cannot read: he strikes the boundary claim, correctly, and then leaves the survey's description of a counting stone as an Imperial march-stone with ornament standing in the Office's register, which is the error on-the-tally-stones made and which he has just proved.

contradicts.on: whether the stones on the third terrace are Imperial boundary stones

books.text:
I have kept a casebook since my first year on the bench at Anvil, for the reason that a judgment which is not written down is a judgment that will be remembered differently by every man who heard it, including the man who gave it; and I have kept this one, which is my fourth, with more care than the others, because the Assize at Gideon is a court whose records the Provincial Office has twice asked to inspect and has twice been refused, and I intend that when it finally compels me there shall be nothing in them I am ashamed of.

A word on the court itself, for whoever reads this after me.

The Assize sits at Gideon in the long room above the customs floor, on the second and fourth weeks, and it hears what the Office sends it and what walks in. That second class is smaller than the first by a great margin and I have never been able to persuade the Office that this is a defect rather than a proof of good order. The room holds forty and is rarely a quarter full. There is a clerk, there is a sworn interpreter of the coastal speech, and there is a second interpreter for the interior tongue whom we have retained for six years and used four times. I record that figure without comment and the reader may do with it what he likes.

The forms are the forms of any provincial assize. A complaint is brought, in writing or by word to the clerk, who writes it. The complaint is read back. The complainant is asked whether it is truly stated, and the answer is entered. The other party is summoned, and if he does not come the second time he is heard against. Evidence is taken on oath, in whichever tongue the witness prefers, and the oath is administered in that tongue by the interpreter, which I insisted upon in my first month here against the settled practice of my predecessor, who administered it in Tamrielic to men who did not speak it and counted that sufficient.

I set down what follows not as precedent, the Assize making none, but as the record of a working year.

THE MATTER OF THE TOLL AT THE QUAY.

A bond-factor of Gideon, Tesserus Bant, complained against a poler of the Gideon quay, one Eeja-Sul, that the said poler had refused carriage after money paid. The poler's answer, taken through the interpreter, was that the money paid was for a boat measured at the keel and the cargo offered was a cargo for a boat measured at the draught, and that he would not take it.

The bond is a printed form and the printed form says keel. I gave for the complainant, in the sum paid and no costs.

I asked the poler, as the form requires, whether he wished to say anything further before the entry was closed. He said that he did not. I record that he said it politely and at once and that he had said the same when asked whether the complaint was truly stated against him, and that in my judgment a man who has a grievance says so when a court asks him twice.

THE MATTER OF THE KILN CAMP ON THE SALT FLATS.

The Office referred a complaint of its own motion, which is the class of case I am sent most often and like least, the Office being both complainant and the body that will act on my finding. The complaint was that the kiln camp above the flats had taken on hands beyond the number entered on its lease, and had not returned them at the term.

The kiln master appeared. His books were produced and they are good books; I say that as a man who has looked at a great many bad ones. The count entered at the start of the term and the count at the end agree, and the difference alleged by the Office arises from a second list in the same hand, headed only with a word I am told means the day's water, which the Office read as a list of persons and which the kiln master says is a list of loads.

I could not decide it on the books and there was no other evidence, none of the hands themselves having come, and I dismissed the complaint without prejudice to its being brought again on better material. The Office has not brought it again.

I have thought since about why no hand came. The clerk sent the summons to the camp in the ordinary way and the ordinary way is a written summons carried by a runner, and I have satisfied myself that the runner went. It has been put to me, by the interpreter, in a conversation I did not ask for and have set down here because it was said seriously, that a summons which arrives written and unread is not a summons at all, and that a man who cannot read it and will not say he cannot read it will do the only thing that leaves his dignity where it was, which is nothing.

I do not accept this. A court cannot be asked to guess who among the persons before it is unable to read, and to begin guessing is to begin deciding who shall be treated as a child. But I have instructed the clerk that summonses out of the city are to be read aloud to the party by the runner and the runner is to enter that he has done so, and I note that we have had two more appearances from the flats since, which may be that and may be the season.

THE MATTER OF THE STONE ON THE THIRD TERRACE.

A survey party of the Ninth Cohort entered a complaint against persons unknown that a boundary stone set by the Office had been thrown down. I went out to look at it, which is not the practice here and ought to be.

The stone is not a boundary stone. It is one of the counting stones of the interior, which stand in lines and are cut with a notation the Office's own survey has three times described as ornament, and it had not been thrown down; it is lying because it has always been lying, and the fourth stone in the line is lying in the same manner and to the same angle, and I would ask any surveyor who has seen two stones fall identically in a marsh to write to me.

I dismissed the complaint and I entered my reason, which is that no offence is disclosed. The Serjeant took it well. He said, and I think he meant it kindly, that the Office had put the stone in its survey as an Imperial march-stone with ornament, and that if I struck it out he would have to explain a hole in the line. I said that a hole in a line is a smaller thing than an error in a register.

He asked me what the notation was a count of. I said that I did not know. He asked me who did, and I said that the persons who cut it presumably had, and he laughed and said that they were four hundred years dead and that in any case no one in the interior would tell an Imperial the time of day.

I have found that last observation to be true, and I have not yet found out why, and I set it down here so that I may come back to it.

books.title: The Casebook of the Assize at Gideon, Volume the Second: Of the Lease
books.author: Justiciar Aulus Merrow, of the Assize at Gideon
books.unreliability: He sets out three explanations for the seventeen missing from the Blackrose yard tally, cannot choose between them on the material, disposes of the referral correctly, and knows it. The volume is a man being right about the law and wrong about what the law is for, in his own words, without a narrator anywhere.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Enters that no offence is disclosed because no complaint was made by or on behalf of any of the seventeen — the persons who might have complained being, on his own three explanations, on the flats, dead, or on a boat. He notices the circularity, writes it down, and holds to the rule anyway.

contradicts.on: whether the lease raises any question of consent

books.text:
The second volume of this book is given almost entirely to the lease, and I would rather it were not, but a casebook is a record of what came and this is what came.

THE STATEMENT OF THE PREFECT.

Before any case of the lease reached me at all, there arrived at the Assize a statement in the hand of Prefect Galvus Arn of Blackrose, addressed to this court, unsolicited, concerning an arrangement about which no complaint had then been made to me by anyone. It is a careful document. It sets out the numbers, it sets out the difficulties before an opponent can, and it distinguishes with some elegance between a lease of labour and a sale of the person, which distinction is good law and which I would myself have drawn in the same words.

I filed it. There was nothing else to do with it, there being no proceeding to file it in.

I record here, because I have been asked about it since and shall be asked again, that I did not treat it as a confession, and that I do not now. A man who writes to a court before he is accused is either a fool or an honest officer who can see what is coming, and Arn is not a fool. But I have read it a fourth time this quarter and I notice what I did not notice at first, which is that every difficulty he raises is a difficulty about counting, and that he raises no difficulty at all about consent, and that this is because it would not occur to him that there was one, and it did not occur to me either.

THE MATTER OF THE HOLDING AT THE SALT FLATS AND THE COUNT RETURNED.

The Office referred the yard tally of Blackrose for the quarter, on the motion of a clerk of that yard whose name is not on the referral and who I am told is no longer at that yard.

The document is short and I set out its substance. Under sentence at the wall, counted at first light on the last day of the quarter: five hundred and twenty-nine. Out on lease, per the lease register: 411. Total, per the register of persons: nine hundred and forty. The arithmetic is correct and the yard signed it.

Beneath it, in a second hand, is the note that brought it here. It says that the flats returned three hundred and ninety-four bodies to the gate that quarter and that the yard signed for three hundred and ninety-four, and that the register was not altered, because the register counts the lease and not the men, and the lease stands at 411 until the term ends. The writer says that he has written to the Prefect and that it is the second time.

The difference is seventeen.

I sat with this for the better part of a day and I set down the ways I found to look at it.

The first is that the seventeen are alive and are on the flats, the term not being ended, and the return of three hundred and ninety-four is a return of those whose work was done. The lease register is then correct and the note is a misreading by a clerk who does not know the instrument. Against this: the note is written by a man who signs for bodies at a gate for his living, and a man does not write twice to a Prefect about an instrument he has misread.

The second is that the seventeen are dead on the flats and have not been reported, which is the difficulty Prefect Arn himself raised in his statement, in terms, and about which he says he has written to the Office three times and holds the copies. If that is so, the offence, if there is one, lies with the holdings, and I have no complainant.

The third is that the seventeen were never returned because they were never to be returned, and that somewhere between the gate and the flats there is a factor, and beyond the factor a keel, and beyond the keel a house in Morrowind where a person may lawfully be held as property because that province's law permits it and this one's does not. Prefect Arn's statement says that some of the holdings are held through factors and that some of those factors hold for houses in Morrowind, and that he has satisfied himself in each case that it is lawful, and that he is aware of what it looks like.

I could not choose between the three on the material before me and I did not.

What I did was this. I entered that no offence was disclosed upon the referral as brought, and I noted, in the entry, that no complaint had been made by or on behalf of any of the seventeen, and that the court could not proceed upon a difference in two registers where no person alleged a wrong.

That is the correct disposal. I have gone over it since and I cannot fault it. A court is not an inquiry; it does not go looking; it answers what is put to it, and nothing was put to me but a subtraction.

I would only observe, and I observe it against myself, that the persons who might have complained were at that time on the flats, or were dead, or were on a boat, and that a rule requiring a man to come to Gideon and speak to a clerk in order to be counted as wronged is a rule that will always find no wrong wherever it is most needed. I do not know what a court is supposed to do about that. I have written the difficulty down, which is what one does with a difficulty one cannot dispose of, and I have not looked at the entry since without discomfort.

THE MATTER OF THE WOMAN WHO CAME ABOUT A NAME.

A woman of the coast came in on an ordinary sitting, without a complaint in the form, and asked the clerk whether a name was in the register of persons. The clerk asked her whose name and she gave one, and he looked, and it was there, in the second part, recorded at Lilmoth. She asked what the third column said. The third column of that leaf is water-damaged and says nothing at all except one word at the foot of the page, in the hand of whoever closed it, and the word is sufficient.

She asked what that meant. The clerk did not know. I did not know. I sent to the Office and the Office replied, after five weeks, that the notation is a clerk's mark of long standing indicating that the entry as made was sufficient for the purpose for which it was made, and that no further record exists.

I gave her that answer in those words, through the interpreter, and she thanked me, and she asked no further question, and she went out.

The interpreter stayed behind and said to me: she will not ask again, and you should understand that this is not because she is satisfied. I asked him what it was, then, and he said that if she asks again she will have said that she believes I am lying to her, and that she would rather not have said it.

I have thought about this more than about anything else in the volume. I hold to the view that a court must take a person at their word and that a person who says nothing has said nothing. But I am obliged to record that I have now twice been told, by a man whose business is the meaning of what people say, that in this province the absence of a complaint is not evidence of the absence of a grievance, and that I have built the greater part of my year's work on the contrary assumption.

I do not propose to change the forms. I propose to write down that I was told.

books.title: The Casebook of the Assize at Gideon, Volume the Third: Of What a Court Can Make Good
books.author: Justiciar Aulus Merrow, lately of the Assize at Gideon, and afterwards of Anvil
books.unreliability: Ends with the author understanding exactly what has been done to him and recording that he did the same thing to his interpreter ten minutes earlier. He is still wrong about the apprenticeship: he treats a witnessed mark as unimpeachable on the ground that the court cannot go behind it, having just been told by the witnessing clerk that no interpreter has ever been present at such a signing.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Declines to order the child returned because the order could not be enforced, and calls that honesty; the Office's reply — that he has substituted his estimate of the province's temper for the law, and that the effect is to tell a subject his right is good and he may not have it — is printed in his own book and he says he has no answer to it.

contradicts.on: whether the interior is governed by the Empire's law

books.text:
This volume is shorter than the others and it is the last, and the reader will see why before the end of it.

THE MATTER OF THE HOLDING AT HOLLOW-REEDS AND THE CHILD.

A holder of the coastal flats, a citizen of this province and of good standing at the chartered market, complained that a child bound to him under an instrument of apprenticeship had been taken out of his house by persons of the interior, and he asked for the child's return.

The instrument was produced and it is regular on its face. It is the printed form, it bears a mark for the parent and the mark is witnessed by a clerk of the Office, and the term is nine years, which is long but is within what the form allows. The holder had paid what the form requires him to pay, which is the keep, and had entered the child in the register of persons as the form requires, and I have no doubt whatever that he believed himself to be, and in every particular of the written law was, entirely in the right.

The persons of the interior did not appear. They were summoned twice, in the manner I described in the first volume, read aloud by the runner and entered as read, and on the second occasion the runner returned with a message that he had been asked to carry and had written down as well as he could, and I have had it rendered by both interpreters, who differ, and I set down both renderings because I am not able to choose between them.

The coastal interpreter gives it: the child was not given and cannot be given, and the mark on your paper is the mark of a woman who was answering a different question.

The interior interpreter gives it: the child was not given and cannot be given, and the mark on your paper was made by a woman who was answering the question you asked, which was not the question you thought you asked.

I do not know whether the difference between those two renderings is a difference in the message or a difference in the two men, and I put that difficulty on the record where it can be seen, because I have come to think that the greater part of what this court does not know is of exactly that kind and that we have no way at all of measuring how much of it there is.

I heard the holder. I heard the clerk of the Office who witnessed the mark, who is a young man, who was straightforward with me, and who told me, when I pressed him, that he had explained the instrument to the woman in Tamrielic, and that she had listened to the whole of it and had then made her mark, and that he had asked her whether she understood and she had said yes; and who told me also, because I asked, that he does not speak the interior tongue, that no interpreter was present, that none was required by the form, and that in his four years at that desk none has ever been present at the signing of an apprenticeship.

I gave judgment as follows.

That the instrument is regular, and that the court cannot go behind a witnessed mark upon the assertion of an absent party, and that upon the material before it the holder's right is made out.

And that the court declines to order the return of the child.

I set out my reason at length in the entry and I shall put the short form of it here. A court orders what it can make good. If I order this child returned, the order will be carried by a runner into the interior, where it will be read aloud to persons who did not come when they were summoned and who will not come now, and it will not be obeyed; and there is no Legion inland, as the Office is proud to tell the province in print, and the Assize has no arm of its own beyond the city and the flats. An order that cannot be enforced is not mercy and it is not law. It is a lie about the reach of this court, published under my name, and I will not put my name to it.

The holder's man asked me whether I was saying that the interior was outside the law. I said that I was saying that it was outside my order. He asked what the difference was. I have written that question down too.

WHAT FOLLOWED.

The Office wrote to me within the month. The letter is courteous throughout and I have kept it. It observes that a Justiciar who declines to make orders on the ground that they will not be obeyed has substituted his own estimate of the province's temper for the law, that the estimate may be right and is not his to make, and that the effect of the judgment, whatever its reasoning, is that a subject of the Empire has been told that his right is good and that he may not have it.

Every word of that is true and I have not found an answer to it in four months of trying.

The letter goes on to say that the Assize at Gideon will be reconstituted at the turn of the year with two justiciars sitting rather than one, which is an improvement I have myself asked for twice, and that I am to be thanked for my service and offered the bench at Anvil, which is my own country and a good court and a smaller one.

I have accepted. I want it understood by whoever keeps this book after me that I do not think I was driven out. I think I was moved, competently, by an officer doing his work, in a manner that leaves everyone able to say the true thing about it, and I think that this is the province's whole method in a sentence and that I have been on the other end of it for a year without recognising it.

A LAST NOTE, WHICH IS NOT A CASE.

On my last sitting the interpreter came up afterwards, the coastal one, who has been at that table longer than any justiciar has sat at this one.

I asked him, because I was going and it cost me nothing, what he would change about the court.

He said: nothing. The court is well kept and the oaths are taken properly and you have been fair, and I would change nothing about it.

I said that this was a great deal of praise and that I had not earned it, and I asked him again, and he said, with the same courtesy, that he would change nothing.

I remembered then what he had told me in the second volume of this book about a woman who did not ask twice, and I understood, standing there, that I had just done to him precisely what the Office does to this province, which is to ask a question in a form that leaves only one polite answer and then to write the answer down as though it were the truth.

I did not ask him a third time. I am aware that this was cowardice and I have decided to record it as such rather than to dress it as tact.

The books of the Assize for the four hundred and twenty-sixth year are complete to this entry and are left in good order for my successor, whose name I do not yet know.
